The Board is ultimately responsible for information security and ensures it is maintained commensurate with the size and extent of threats, enabling continued sound operation
Information security roles and responsibilities of the Board, senior management, governing bodies and individuals (decision-making, approval, oversight, operations) are clearly defined
An information security capability commensurate with the size and extent of threats to information assets is maintained
The information security capability of each related party or third party managing information assets is assessed, commensurate with the potential consequences of an incident
The capability is actively maintained against changes in vulnerabilities and threats, including from changes to information assets or the business environment
An information security policy framework commensurate with exposures to vulnerabilities and threats is maintained
The policy framework provides direction on the responsibilities of all parties obliged to maintain information security (staff, contractors, consultants, related and third parties, customers)
Information assets, including those managed by related and third parties, are classified by criticality and sensitivity reflecting the potential financial and non-financial impact of an incident

Information security controls protect information assets, implemented in a timely manner and commensurate with vulnerabilities and threats, criticality and sensitivity, life-cycle stage, and the potential consequences of an incident
The design of each related party's or third party's information security controls protecting the entity's information assets is evaluated
Robust mechanisms detect and respond to information security incidents in a timely manner
Information security response plans are maintained for incidents that could plausibly occur
Response plans include mechanisms for managing all stages from detection to post-incident review, and for escalation and reporting to the Board, governing bodies and responsible individuals
Information security response plans are reviewed and tested annually to ensure they remain effective and fit-for-purpose

Control effectiveness is tested through a systematic testing program whose nature and frequency match the rate of change in threats, asset criticality and sensitivity, incident consequences, exposure to untrusted environments, and the materiality and frequency of change
Where reliance is placed on a related party's or third party's control testing, the nature and frequency of that testing is assessed against paragraph 27(a)–(e)
Testing results that identify control deficiencies which cannot be remediated in a timely manner are escalated and reported to the Board or senior management
Testing is conducted by appropriately skilled and functionally independent specialists
The sufficiency of the testing program is reviewed at least annually or on material change to information assets or the business environment
Internal audit reviews the design and operating effectiveness of information security controls, including those maintained by related and third parties (control assurance)
Information security control assurance is provided by appropriately skilled personnel
Internal audit assesses control assurance provided by a related or third party where an incident could materially affect the entity or its customers and audit intends to rely on that assurance

APRA is notified as soon as possible and no later than 72 hours after becoming aware of an information security incident that materially affected (or could materially affect) the entity or its customers, or that was notified to another regulator
APRA is notified as soon as possible and no later than 10 business days after becoming aware of a material control weakness the entity expects not to remediate in a timely manner

The board establishes and approves a technology risk appetite aligned with the institution's risk appetite: risk tolerances for technology events, a risk owner and residual-risk acceptance criteria and authority, key risk indicators, sufficient resources, and regular review

The board approves and reviews IT and cybersecurity strategic plans of at least three years, endorses and oversees the TRMF and CRF, requires robust risk assessments for critical systems and emerging technology, has IT frameworks and policies reviewed at least every three years, and ensures the framework supports technology applications to the Bank
A board-level committee with at least one member with technology experience and competencies oversees technology matters

The board obtains regular updates on technology and cyber threats, allocates time to discuss cyber risks including extreme-incident impacts with external expert input where appropriate, and participates in cybersecurity awareness and training

The board audit committee ensures the effectiveness of the internal technology audit function: competent audit staff, appropriate scope, procedures and frequency, and prompt closure of corrective actions

Senior management implements the TRMF and CRF as policies and procedures consistent with risk appetite, ensures the crisis management plan escalates recovery considering duration, customers affected and transactions impacted, and reports KPIs and risk controls to the board regularly

A cross-functional committee of cyber, technology and business senior management oversees the strategic technology plan and policies, updates the board on key technology matters, and approves policy deviations after risk assessment, reporting material deviations to the board
The technology risk management framework (TRMF) is an integral part of the enterprise risk management framework

The TRMF defines technology risk, assigns responsibilities with governance and reporting, identifies risks including emerging technology, classifies all information assets by criticality, sets measurement and assessment methods, controls and mitigations, continuous monitoring, an accurate risk profile, key resources and interdependencies including critical third parties and their connected parties, scenario analysis for severe conditions, and incident management to restore services to a secure and stable state

An independent enterprise-wide technology risk management function implements the TRMF and CRF, advises on critical technology projects and escalates critical issues, and gives independent views on third-party assessments

A designated CISO with sufficient authority, independence and resources is independent of day-to-day operations, apprises the board and senior management of current and emerging technology risks, has the requisite technical, audit, governance, risk, strategic and third-party-risk skills, and is appropriately certified

The CISO formulates policies implementing the TRMF and CRF, enforces compliance with them and with technology regulatory requirements, and advises senior management on technology risk and security matters
Technology project governance is commensurate with risk and complexity: oversight roles, authority and reporting structures, and risk assessments throughout the project life cycle

Project risk assessments address resource adequacy including vendors and concurrent projects, system complexity and integration, security controls through the life cycle, completeness of user requirements, robustness of testing, deployment and fallback strategies, and disaster recovery readiness
The board and senior management receive and review timely reports on significant project risks throughout implementation

An enterprise technology architecture framework gives a comprehensive view of technology and baseline components, a technical design showing infrastructure, interconnectivity, dependencies and security controls (to find single points of failure), mappings to business functions, units, applications and data, principles for network and security design, and longer-term priorities

An SDLC methodology covers requirement, design, development, testing, deployment, change management, maintenance and decommissioning, integrated with enterprise architecture, risk management and security principles including segregation of duties

Rapid development (DevOps) meets enterprise security, governance and compliance requirements, with automated IT security compliance review and automated vulnerability discovery and testing before release
Production is physically segregated from development and testing; on cloud, these environments do not run on the same virtual host
Rigorous system testing precedes deployment, verifying user requirements and robustness; sensitive test data requires authorisation and disclosure safeguards
Changes to source code of critical systems undergo source code review for security and recognised coding practices before introduction
System changes are independently reviewed and approved; contingency plans for unsuccessful material changes are established and tested

Contracts for critical systems developed or maintained by third parties require sufficient notice of impacting changes, demonstrated secure-by-design development, and continued accessibility of source code for business continuity
Decommissioning of critical systems minimises customer and business impact, with contingency plans established and tested for unsuccessful decommissioning
Robust policies identify and reduce shadow IT risks

No system or digital service runs with known security vulnerabilities, on outdated platforms or end-of-life technology: a current security hardening baseline, timely patching, remedial plans for approaching EOL, and management-approved, risk-assessed, annually reviewed exceptions with phase-out timelines

A patch and EOL management framework covers asset identification and risk assessment, deployment criteria, priority and turnaround by severity, compatibility testing, an end-to-end approval, testing, monitoring and tracking workflow, and end-user awareness

The effectiveness and security of technology in use is monitored against disruptive developments (e.g. quantum computing): board advice on impact, a long-term strategy with competent resources, and a migration roadmap

A cryptography policy requires industry-standard algorithms, message authentication, hashes, signatures and random number generation; secure key life-cycle management; at least annual review of standards and algorithms for critical and customer-facing systems; an asset inventory of cryptographic tools and algorithms with rationale and mappings; and tested compromise-recovery plans

Cryptographic controls are evaluated with due diligence; the institution retains ownership and control of encryption keys (or with an independent custodian) except for non-critical systems without customer information, manages externally generated keys to industry standards, weighs reliance on third-party assessments against risk appetite, and considers resource impact and reduced traffic visibility

Cryptographic protocols for secret and public keys follow recognised international standards and are tested; secret and private key storage and computation occur in a protected environment (HSM, TEE or equivalent) commensurate with risk

Public keys are stored in certificates from a Certificate Authority (recognised CAs for customers); authentication and signature protocols protect private keys so their use is legally binding; issuance and renewal follow industry and legal specifications
Resilience and availability objectives of data centres are specified to support business recovery objectives
Data centres have redundant capacity components and multiple distribution paths with no single point of failure

Critical systems are hosted in dedicated, physically secured production data centre space not in a disaster-prone area, with no single point of failure in hardware, electrical, thermal and infrastructure design, and with adequate maintenance and continuous monitoring with timely alerts
Data centre operations have control procedures including automated batch management, production change procedures, error handling and exception management
Incompatible activities in data centre operations are segregated (development from operations); necessary vendor or programmer access to production is authorised and monitored
System capacity is planned and managed for peak periods, growth plans and architecture changes
Real-time monitoring tracks capacity utilisation and performance of key processes and services with actionable alerts; scope, metrics and thresholds are updated periodically

Key digital services and delivery channels are made resilient: early-warning mechanisms by 30 September 2027 (detect failed transactions and measure availability, monitor affected customers and volumes, escalate immediately when 5% or more of expected daily customers or transactions are affected), regular reviews of vulnerable interdependencies, and stand-in processing arrangements by 30 September 2027 prioritised for the least substitutable channels with customers informed of terms, risks and responsibilities

Critical systems with an expectation of immediate customer or counterparty service are designed for high availability: cumulative unplanned downtime at the customer interface of not more than 4 hours on a rolling 12 months and a maximum tolerable downtime of 120 minutes per incident
Diversity in technology is prioritised so critical systems infrastructure is not excessively exposed to similar technology risks

During digital service interruptions the institution escalates and decides promptly to resume via alternatives within the 10.32 timeframe, defines accountabilities and third-party arrangements for degradation, runs a communication plan with immediate customer notice, feedback handling, frequent updates and alternatives, offers a convenient availability-status check (e.g. real-time status on the website), and discloses its quarterly availability track record within 15 calendar days of quarter-end from 15 October 2027
A reliable, scalable and secure enterprise network supports business activities and growth plans
Network services for critical systems are reliable with no single point of failure against network faults and cyber threats
Real-time bandwidth monitoring and network resilience metrics flag over-utilisation and disruptions from congestion and faults, including traffic analysis for trends and anomalies
Network services supporting critical systems ensure confidentiality, integrity and availability of data
A maintained network design blueprint identifies all internal and external interfaces and connectivity, physical and logical, with segmentation
Sufficient network device logs are retained for investigation and forensics for at least three years
Safeguards (e.g. logical network segmentation from other group entities) minimise the risk of a compromise in one entity affecting others in the group

A backup strategy and procedures manage the backup life cycle, keep adequate copies of critical data, OS, programs, utilities, master and transaction files and event logs, store media in an environmentally secure access-controlled site, secure removable media per Appendix 1, test restoration periodically with prompt root-cause remediation, and have an independent risk assessment of end-to-end backup storage and delivery
A tamper-proof backup arrangement and an isolated recovery environment enable resumption of critical banking and payment services within tolerance after destructive cyber attacks such as ransomware
The board and senior management exercise effective oversight of third-party service providers for critical technology functions; the institution remains accountable for all resulting risks
Due diligence on third-party service providers is conducted before on-boarding and throughout the engagement, considering at least the Appendix 8 risks

Service level agreements with third-party providers include regulator and institution access rights to records and decision minutes, prior notice of substantial sub-contracting, a secrecy undertaking surviving the engagement, disaster recovery and backup, uptime objectives, exit and termination continuity with timely data recovery, prompt disclosure of disruptions and cyber incidents in the provider's or sub-contractors' environment, compliance with international standards and staff certification, and participation in security awareness programmes

A roadmap achieves continuous monitoring of third-party cybersecurity posture: measuring the infrastructure footprint and customer information accessible to third parties, leading product-specific controls, incident response protocols with providers for software-update vulnerabilities, a priority set of controls with frequent assurance assertions, higher-frequency monitoring of disclosed incidents, automated metric testing, and response to breached thresholds

A comprehensive risk assessment precedes cloud adoption, addressing deployment model sophistication, migration, infrastructure location and geopolitical and legal risk, multi-tenancy and data co-mingling, lock-in and portability, security configurability, exposure via the provider, termination and data recovery, demarcation of responsibilities and liability, and continuing regulatory and standards compliance

Customer, counterparty and proprietary data on cloud services are safeguarded against unauthorised disclosure and access, with ownership, control and management of all such data and services retained, including cryptographic key management
An access control policy governs identification, authentication and authorisation of all users to IT assets and data, with granularity commensurate with unauthorised-access risk

Access control adheres to deny-all by default, least privilege on a need-to-have basis, time-bound access, segregation of incompatible functions (development vs operations, security vs system administration, network operation vs network security, IT operations), dual-authorisation criteria, and authentication by criticality: stronger for critical activities and remote access, robust identity verification at provisioning, and credentials uniquely linked to one user
Multi-factor authentication resistant to social engineering, combining two or more of knowledge, inherent and possession factors, authenticates user access to critical systems
A user access matrix outlines access rights, roles or profiles and the authorising and approving authorities, reviewed and updated periodically

Access controls to enterprise-wide systems are managed and monitored, anomalies are flagged for prompt investigation, and user activities in critical systems are logged, retained at least three years and reviewed in a timely manner
Cyber risk management has an enterprise-wide focus reflecting the collective responsibility of business and technology lines

A cyber resilience framework (CRF) articulates governance, resilience objectives and risk tolerance against the evolving threat environment, targets operational resilience against extreme but plausible attacks, and supports identification, protection, detection, response and recovery of on-premises and third-party-hosted systems and data

The CRF includes institutional understanding of cyber risk context and posture; identification, classification and prioritisation of critical systems, information, assets and interconnectivity; threats, vulnerabilities and countermeasures; layered defence with zero-trust, micro-segmentation and security by design; continuous surveillance for timely detection; incident handling procedures and a crisis response playbook; secure information sharing with other institutions and FMIs; a centralised automated technology asset inventory; and a cyber risk management function escalating high-risk threats to senior management and the board
As a designated National Critical Information Infrastructure entity, the institution complies with the Cyber Security Act 2024 requirements, guidelines and NACSA directives and standards
The Appendix 5 control measures are adopted to enhance resilience to cyber attacks
A realistic red-team simulation attack on the infrastructure is conducted at least once every three years

Cybersecurity operations have clear responsibilities with mitigating measures for each phase of the attack life cycle: reconnaissance, weaponisation, delivery, exploitation, installation, command and control, exfiltration

Continuous proactive monitoring and timely detection of anomalies via a Security Operations Centre with competent resources and tools, covering all critical systems and supporting infrastructure, with regular vulnerability assessment and penetration testing per Appendix 5

A cyber threat intelligence process collects, analyses and evaluates threat information including data breaches and misleading information about the institution on the Internet, social media and dark web
Flagged anomalous activities are investigated and responded to according to their complexity

Cyber crisis management policies and procedures incorporate attack scenarios and responses into the crisis management plan, escalation, BCP and DR, with a communication plan for shareholders, regulators, customers and employees

A Cyber Incident Response Plan covers preparedness (CERT governance, reporting, roles, invocation and escalation), detection and analysis (points of compromise, damage assessment including threat-actor claims, evidence preservation), containment and eradication, recovery with contingency strategies, and post-incident review with lessons learned
CERT members are conversant with the incident response plan and procedures and remain contactable at all times
A secure, reliable out-of-band communication infrastructure for internal and external stakeholders operates if primary communications are compromised

An annual cyber drill tests the CIRP and out-of-band communications on current and emerging scenarios with the board, senior management and relevant third parties, covering escalation, communication and decision-making at different impact levels and the readiness of CERT and third parties; results are reported to the board

Loss provision arrangements are reviewed against scenario analysis of extreme cyber events; any cyber insurance adequately covers the events and liabilities, its warranties and obligations are reflected in crisis procedures without unintended exclusions, and insurer obligations do not impair acting in the institution's and customers' best interests
Cyber incidents are notified to the Bank per the Operational Risk Reporting, Business Continuity Management and Merchant Acquiring Services policy documents and any other specified policy
Cyber threat intelligence is shared with the industry on a timely basis via the Bank's, industry's or law enforcement platforms, with resources allocated to industry-wide intelligence initiatives
The institution collaborates and cooperates closely with relevant stakeholders and authorities in combating cyber threats

The CRF implements robust security controls for digital services: minimum controls per delivery channel assessed regularly (Appendices 2, 3, 4, 11), proper user and device authentication and transaction authorisation against impersonation and fraud (Appendix 3), and strong physical and logical controls

Where the §12 digital services controls are not yet implemented, documented explanation shows alternatives are at least as effective and the institution assumes liability for fraud arising from the gap

The CRF extends to customers' mobile devices and access points: layered controls protecting the mobile application and its data, continuous surveillance of exploitation with swift control upgrades, incident handling to help customers contain damage, coordinated rapid countermeasure upgrades across functions, senior management review with escalation thresholds, and board apprisal of outcomes
Fraud detection capabilities and rules are updated promptly on new modus operandi, supported by risk analytics and continuous upgrade per Appendix 11 Fraud Detection Standards

Digital service delivery risks are mitigated: secure communication channels with compensating controls for phishing-prone channels (no clickable links in SMS), advance customer information on new controls, and practical ways for customers to verify calls from the institution or its outsourced providers
Customers can manage activation and de-activation of payment cards for card-not-present and overseas transactions, without diminishing the institution's liabilities and duty of care

Customer awareness programmes are continuously reviewed for effectiveness: timely practical fraud-identification information including new modus operandi, clear explanation of security measures and how to verify genuine sites and apps, real-time alerts when measures are absent, and measures such as interactive simulations

Customers can conveniently report, suspend and re-activate accounts on suspected fraud: a secure self-service kill switch, an adequately resourced contact centre, and restoration of access within a reasonable time after validation

Incidents involving potential fraud or compromised customer data trigger heightened monitoring of affected accounts, notification of affected customers with mitigation information, and revocation and re-issue of affected credentials or payment instruments where exploitation risk exists
Scope, frequency and intensity of technology audits are commensurate with the complexity, sophistication and criticality of systems and applications

The technology audit plan is reviewed annually with appropriate frequency and coverage of critical services, third-party providers, material external interfaces, delayed or terminated critical projects, and post-implementation reviews of new or material enhancements
Internal audit has dedicated, specialised, professionally certified technology audit resources conversant with the institution's systems and delivery channels

A technically competent external provider performs a production data centre resilience and risk assessment (DCRA) at least every three years or on material change, covering paragraphs 10.24–10.28; reliance on third-party reports for provider-managed data centres is consistent with risk appetite and meets the same requirements; the board-level committee deliberates the outcome

A technically competent external provider performs network resilience and risk assessments (NRA) at least every three years or on material network design change, covering paragraphs 10.36–10.43; the board-level committee deliberates the outcome

Regular technology and cybersecurity awareness education for all staff is conducted at least annually, reflects the evolving threat landscape, is measured for effectiveness, and includes third-party providers where appropriate
Staff in technology operations, cybersecurity and risk management receive adequate continuous training and are competent and suitably certified
Board members receive regular training and information on technology developments to discharge their oversight role
